item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now.
The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.
But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.
I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.
With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

big boy
warm tension, cold chills heart hanging off a cliff, ready to free fall floating in space with no love, just me and some stranger souls wearing smiles and greet “How are you?” “I’m good, you?”
life carries on, unhinged a tear slips, no one noticed vision blurs, drowned in thoughts what a strange grown-up world
i asked my inner child, why do you live? he has never thought about it he slid on the cold iced river, amused he sang, he played, he drew he flew into the unknown, fearless, curious he closed his eyes and saw wonders
like water, with no shape like paper, clear of rules
“Why cry, big boy?” “You are still me, and I’m still you.”

item.title: State of AI 2026: The Biggest Stories of the Year (and AGI in 2027?) | Nathan Benaich
item.description:
播客：The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18 The cyber risk is, like, much more real than, like, AI exterminating humanity. You either, like, die trying to get to the frontier or you just live long enough to eventually serve inference. Individuals would prefer to live next to a nuclear power plant than live next to a data center. It's bananas what's happened in the last year alone, so let's see AGI next year.
Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:54 That is Nathan Beneche, venture capitalist and author of the State of AI Report. Every year, Nathan and his team compile all the key facts, figures, trends of the AI industry into a 250 slide report that is one of my favorite reads and reference documents. Nathan is back for a third time on this show and as usual, we covered many of the stories of the year as well as some of his predictions. Why AGI could happen in 2027, AI that is now building AI, what really happened in the Hugging Face incident, the data center backlash, and how he runs his own fund on agents. I'm Matt Turk, and this is the MAD Podcast.
Speaker 2 | 00:56 - 01:16 So every year, you do this big report that we're going to extensively talk about, and you end the report with predictions. And, like, historically, your predictions have been somewhat measured, but this year, you went all out. And the the last prediction is AGI 2027. So, why is that? Unpack that for us.
Speaker 1 | 01:16 - 01:36 Yeah. I mean, it's been like ten years roughly speaking of writing this report. And, you know, originally it was like a year is like long enough time that enough stuff happens that you have, you know, enough content to write the report. And honestly, like this year was really, really hectic. Every other day towards the end of the timeline for publishing, which was like October 8, I had to make updates.
Speaker 1 | 01:36 - 02:07 And there was a point where I was like, please, just like no more news over like one day that I can at least record my like launch video, etcetera. So by the time I was like making the predictions and, you know, I went through a few like scary cybersecurity ones, which I guess only got worse in the last couple of weeks. Just the experience of just seeing like everybody else who's using these products, just like rapid capability improvement, you know, week after week. And I think there's many, many use cases I have now where like, I think the model is like brilliant. I'm particularly like an astro boy.
Speaker 1 | 02:07 - 02:29 I really love that system. And I could see like in the next twelve months that whether it's, you know, legal finance, like my investment job, like thinking intelligently about topics I don't know that the model could potentially be like better than what I could do in any, you know, compressed amount of time that I have to do the work. And so for me, that would be like approximately AGI.
Speaker 2 | 02:29 - 02:46 Yeah. And a big theme of the year that you highlight in the report is RSI, recursive self improvement, which is this idea of AI building AI, which we've discussed extensively on this podcast throughout the episodes. Is that part of the story that would accelerate us towards AGI for you?
Speaker 1 | 02:46 - 03:26 Yeah. I think so. Right now, the challenge is, like, how do you frame problems that the model is currently not good at in a way that is amenable to RSI, which would be, you know, potentially having like a software environment that approximates the task on the computer or some kind of verifiable reward, which I'm sure you've discussed a lot about. And I think if we can get to a point where in like any arbitrary domain, we're just limited by the amount of compute and synthetic data we can generate, then then, yeah, for like most knowledge work, which I I I do think to some degree that's that's possible, particularly as like models get better as as their own verifiers. That would be one of the main reasons why AGI would come would come faster.
Speaker 2 | 03:26 - 03:36 Yep. You had some stats that you mentioned in the report from Anthropic where they say Claude leads 26% of its measured model R and D in August.
Speaker 1 | 03:36 - 03:45 Yeah. Yeah. Exactly. And that's like I think up from 1% a couple of months ago and that was August, which sounds really far away. So God knows what it is in October.
Speaker 1 | 03:46 - 04:24 And so there's that I think that was that was really interesting. But then there was there was another... A stat that I really liked from a blog post that they had in June this year about recursive self improvement, which explained the concept. Then they presented this kind of dual arm experiment where they were testing out different model generations versus a human in this setup where first the human would undertake a research agenda and, you know, go a couple of steps down this path deciding what to work on doing the work. And then at some point, that experiment would fork and the human would continue or a specific model generation would continue.
Speaker 1 | 04:24 - 05:15 And it would be, you know, the old sonnet versions to Opus and then Fable. And then and the experiment would end and human graders would look at the human path versus the model path. And it was something like the old generation of models humans preferred like 10% of the time or something like that. But for the Mithos class models, humans preferred that research direction 64% of the time, which suggests that models are getting better at predicting the right steps or the right interesting kind of, you know, sort of leafs in the in the nodes to pursue. And then the second kind of piece of data I liked was some research from OpenAI with their codex usage amongst their AI staff where they tried to classify the sort of token use in the overall process of their of their research.
Speaker 1 | 05:15 - 06:14 And that would be using tokens for deciding what research question to test, how to test it, what experiment you should set up, like writing the training code, running the, you know, the data engineering pipelines, writing the infrastructure, etcetera, and then marketing the paper, writing the paper, etcetera. And the vast majority of the token usage was on kind of explaining the research writing, which kind of makes sense, you know, sort of knowledge work followed by all the infrastructure for running the experiment. Very, very few tokens were used for what question should I explore and like, why should I explore it and what's the right path? And so I like this question a lot because like I was trained in science and biology and I just remember, you know, this is like ten years ago, fifteen years ago, not that long. But you know, at the start of the PhD, you would sit there with, you know, a ton of papers and you know, you go on the internet and read, read, read, read, read, try to understand what's the status quo, how do people test certain ideas, where are the gaps, what experiment should I run, and then in concert with your supervisor, like decide on the path.
Speaker 1 | 06:14 - 06:41 And the best supervisors would be the ones who could guide you down the most fruitful path to get hopefully your nature paper and then off you were. And the worst supervisors were the ones that like didn't really know or didn't have great ideas. So that idea of like research taste, which is what kind of gets bandied around on Twitter a lot is I think one of the hallmarks of intelligence and is one of the critical components towards RSI working well and is one that I just like really enjoy because it speaks to my interest in science.
Speaker 2 | 06:41 - 06:55 Yeah. Indeed taste is sort of become a cliched Yeah. Word over the last couple of years. But in the specific context of RSI, just to play back what you just said, it's effectively choosing the right problem. Yeah.
Speaker 2 | 06:55 - 06:57 That's the right Yeah
Speaker 1 | 06:57 - 07:19 exactly and you know a lot of famous inventors will say you know it's like invention is a result out ...
